Pareto Distribution

Overview¶

How quickly does the chance of a large observation fall as we raise the threshold? The Pareto law models a positive quantity above a lower cutoff. Its tail exponent α\alphaα controls that rate: smaller exponents give more probability to very large observations. Doubling any threshold in its support multiplies the survival probability by 2−α2^{-\alpha}2−α.

Basic probability and integration are enough for this page. A survival probability means P(X>x)\mathbb P(X>x)P(X>x). The formulas below define the CDF FFF, density fff, and quantile QQQ; the survival table illustrates the exponent.

Definition and formula summary¶

Let XXX be a positive random variable with lower cutoff xm>0x_m>0xm​>0 and tail exponent α>0\alpha>0α>0. The Pareto Type I distribution is defined by

Fˉ(x)=P(X>x)={1,x<xm,(xmx)α,x≥xm.\bar F(x)=\mathbb P(X>x)= \begin{cases} 1, & x < x_m,\\ \left(\frac{x_m}{x}\right)^\alpha, & x\ge x_m. \end{cases}Fˉ(x)=P(X>x)={1,(xxm​​)α,​x<xm​,x≥xm​.​
(1)

For x≥xmx\ge x_mx≥xm​, the CDF, density, and quantile function are

F(x)=1−(xmx)α,f(x)=αxmαx−(α+1),Q(q)=xm(1−q)−1/α,0<q<1.F(x)=1-\left(\frac{x_m}{x}\right)^\alpha, \qquad f(x)=\alpha x_m^\alpha x^{-(\alpha+1)}, \qquad Q(q)=x_m(1-q)^{-1/\alpha},\quad 0<q<1.F(x)=1−(xxm​​)α,f(x)=αxmα​x−(α+1),Q(q)=xm​(1−q)−1/α,0<q<1.
(2)

The exact Pareto tail is regularly varying with index −α-\alpha−α. Its raw moment of order p>0p>0p>0 exists exactly when p<αp<\alphap<α:

E[Xp]=αxmpα−p,p<α.\mathbb E[X^p]=\frac{\alpha x_m^p}{\alpha-p},\qquad p<\alpha.E[Xp]=α−pαxmp​​,p<α.
(3)

In particular,

E[X]=αxmα−1,α>1,\mathbb E[X]=\frac{\alpha x_m}{\alpha-1},\qquad \alpha>1,E[X]=α−1αxm​​,α>1,
(4)

and

Var⁡(X)=αxm2(α−1)2(α−2),α>2.\operatorname{Var}(X) =\frac{\alpha x_m^2}{(\alpha-1)^2(\alpha-2)},\qquad \alpha>2.Var(X)=(α−1)2(α−2)αxm2​​,α>2.
(5)

Thus the mean exists only for α>1\alpha>1α>1, and a finite variance exists only for α>2\alpha>2α>2. Here ppp is the moment order and qqq is the quantile level.

Shape and tail intuition¶

Above its lower cutoff, the Pareto law has no characteristic upper scale. Once both thresholds lie in the Pareto tail, multiplying the threshold by a fixed factor changes the exceedance probability by a fixed power:

Fˉ(tx)Fˉ(x)=t−α,t>0,  x≥xm,  tx≥xm.\frac{\bar F(tx)}{\bar F(x)}=t^{-\alpha},\qquad t>0,\; x\ge x_m,\; tx\ge x_m.Fˉ(x)Fˉ(tx)​=t−α,t>0,x≥xm​,tx≥xm​.
(6)

Smaller α\alphaα gives a larger exceedance probability at every x>xmx>x_mx>xm​. The consequences for sums depend on whether the sample size or the exceedance threshold grows; moment existence also depends on the moment order.

The density also shows how the distribution piles mass near the lower cutoff while leaving a long right tail. Its values and scaling make this explicit.

At the cutoff, f(xm)=α/xmf(x_m)=\alpha/x_mf(xm​)=α/xm​. For x≥xmx\ge x_mx≥xm​,

f(2x)f(x)=2−(α+1).\frac{f(2x)}{f(x)}=2^{-(\alpha+1)}.f(x)f(2x)​=2−(α+1).
(7)

This density exponent differs by one from the survival exponent.

Larger α\alphaα concentrates more mass near xmx_mxm​ and makes the density decay faster. Smaller α\alphaα keeps more visible mass far from the cutoff.

The card uses pareto_type1. Regenerate it with uv run python demos/incerto/distribution_cards.py.

Power-law survival¶

Survival probabilities are usually more revealing than densities for fat-tail work. For an exact Pareto law,

Fˉ(x)=xmαx−α,x≥xm,\bar F(x)=x_m^\alpha x^{-\alpha},\qquad x\ge x_m,Fˉ(x)=xmα​x−α,x≥xm​,
(8)

so a log-log survival plot is a straight line with slope −α-\alpha−α:

log⁡Fˉ(x)=αlog⁡xm−αlog⁡x.\log \bar F(x)=\alpha\log x_m-\alpha\log x.logFˉ(x)=αlogxm​−αlogx.
(9)

For xm=1x_m=1xm​=1, the survival values are powers of the threshold:

Tail exponent α\alphaαFˉ(1)\bar F(1)Fˉ(1)Fˉ(2)\bar F(2)Fˉ(2)Fˉ(4)\bar F(4)Fˉ(4)
0.812-0.82-1.6
1.512-1.52-3
312-32-6

These survival functions trace straight lines on log-log axes because each is an exact power. The heaviest tail has the shallowest line.

The same scaling appears numerically. For a fixed multiplier t>0t>0t>0, the ratio Fˉ(tx)/Fˉ(x)\bar F(tx)/\bar F(x)Fˉ(tx)/Fˉ(x) depends only on ttt, provided both x≥xmx\ge x_mx≥xm​ and tx≥xmtx\ge x_mtx≥xm​. The identity follows by canceling (xm/x)α(x_m/x)^\alpha(xm​/x)α.

For example, with α=1.16\alpha=1.16α=1.16, doubling any threshold in the support multiplies survival by 2−1.16≈0.44752^{-1.16}\approx0.44752−1.16≈0.4475. This is a direct evaluation of the scaling identity, not an empirical estimate.

Moment thresholds¶

For a positive moment order ppp, the exact Pareto formula is

E[Xp]=αxmpα−p(p<α),\mathbb E[X^p]=\frac{\alpha x_m^p}{\alpha-p}\quad (p<\alpha),E[Xp]=α−pαxmp​​(p<α),
(10)

and the moment is infinite for p≥αp\ge\alphap≥α. The Pareto moment theorem gives the direct integration proof and the truncated-moment formulas and table. Truncation makes each truncated population moment finite: raising the upper cutoff reveals whether it approaches a limit, grows logarithmically at p=αp=\alphap=α, or grows as a power for p>αp>\alphap>α.

For a general regularly varying tail, Fˉ(x)=x−αL(x)\bar F(x)=x^{-\alpha}L(x)Fˉ(x)=x−αL(x), the boundary p=αp=\alphap=α depends on LLL. Karamata’s theorem explains this distinction; the exact Pareto boundary always diverges.

The moment-existence thresholds give a concrete example:

With xm=1x_m=1xm​=1 and α=1.16\alpha=1.16α=1.16, the mean is 1.16/(1.16−1)=7.251.16/(1.16-1)=7.251.16/(1.16−1)=7.25 and the second raw moment is infinite; the variance is therefore infinite.

For simulation, inverse transform sampling gives

X=xmU−1/α,U∼Uniform⁡(0,1).X=x_m U^{-1/\alpha},\qquad U\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1).X=xm​U−1/α,U∼Uniform(0,1).
(11)

When xmx_mxm​ is known and the observations are independent and identically distributed exact Pareto draws, the maximum-likelihood estimator is

α^=n∑i=1nlog⁡(Xi/xm).\widehat\alpha=\frac{n}{\sum_{i=1}^n\log(X_i/x_m)}.α=∑i=1n​log(Xi​/xm​)n​.
(12)

This formula requires a positive denominator, which holds almost surely under the continuous model. If every observation equals xmx_mxm​, the likelihood has no finite maximizer; it increases as α→∞\alpha\to\inftyα→∞.

This estimator is not a license to fit an exact Pareto from the sample minimum: empirical tail thresholds are rarely known and must be diagnosed separately.

The symmetric shifted double Pareto model extends the tail construction to signed observations.

Exceedance probability and exceedance size¶

For u≥xmu\ge x_mu≥xm​ and y≥0y\ge0y≥0, cancellation of Pareto survival probabilities proves the conditional excess law:

P(X−u>y∣X>u)=Fˉ(u+y)Fˉ(u)=(1+yu)−α.P(X-u>y\mid X>u)=\frac{\bar F(u+y)}{\bar F(u)} =\left(1+\frac yu\right)^{-\alpha}.P(X−u>y∣X>u)=Fˉ(u)Fˉ(u+y)​=(1+uy​)−α.
(13)

This is an exact generalized Pareto survival with shape ξ=1/α\xi=1/\alphaξ=1/α and scale u/αu/\alphau/α. It holds at every threshold u≥xmu\ge x_mu≥xm​ for this model; no limiting approximation is required. Integrating the nonnegative excess survival gives

e(u)=E[X−u∣X>u]=uα−1,E[X∣X>u]=αuα−1,α>1.e(u)=\mathbb E[X-u\mid X>u]=\frac{u}{\alpha-1},\qquad \mathbb E[X\mid X>u]=\frac{\alpha u}{\alpha-1},\quad \alpha>1.e(u)=E[X−u∣X>u]=α−1u​,E[X∣X>u]=α−1αu​,α>1.
(14)

Both expectations are infinite for 0<α≤10<\alpha\le10<α≤1, since the integral of (1+y/u)−α(1+y/u)^{-\alpha}(1+y/u)−α diverges. The first expectation is the mean excess; the second includes the threshold itself. In particular, their ratio to uuu is different.

We also prove the distinction between tail probability and tail contribution to the mean. For any nonnegative XXX and u≥0u\ge0u≥0, the pointwise identity X1{X>u}=u1{X>u}+(X−u)+X\mathbf1_{\{X>u\}}=u\mathbf1_{\{X>u\}}+(X-u)_+X1{X>u}​=u1{X>u}​+(X−u)+​ and Tonelli’s theorem give

E[X1{X>u}]=uFˉ(u)+∫u∞Fˉ(v) dv.\mathbb E[X\mathbf1_{\{X>u\}}] =u\bar F(u)+\int_u^\infty\bar F(v)\,dv.E[X1{X>u}​]=uFˉ(u)+∫u∞​Fˉ(v)dv.
(15)

The equality holds in the extended nonnegative reals, including atoms at uuu. For Pareto with α>1\alpha>1α>1 and u≥xmu\ge x_mu≥xm​ it becomes Fˉ(u)αu/(α−1)\bar F(u)\alpha u/(\alpha-1)Fˉ(u)αu/(α−1). For α=3/2\alpha=3/2α=3/2, xm=1x_m=1xm​=1, and u=4u=4u=4, the probability is 1/81/81/8, the mean excess is 8, the conditional mean is 12, and the tail contribution is 3/23/23/2. Replacing that contribution by uFˉ(u)=1/2u\bar F(u)=1/2uFˉ(u)=1/2 would discard the entire excess integral.

Use pareto_tail_quantities.

Code
from xmath.incerto.glossary import pareto_tail_quantities

for alpha in (1, 1.5, 3):
    print(f"alpha={alpha:.4g}")
    for name, value in pareto_tail_quantities(alpha, x_m=1, threshold=4).items():
        print(f"  {name}: {value:.4g}")

These definitions clarify SCoFT v4 §2.2.4, pp. 10–11, and §§2.2.23–24, pp. 17–18 Taleb, 2025. The exact Pareto calculation here does not classify arbitrary tails from a finite mean-excess plot. Reproduce it with uv run python demos/incerto/glossary_worked_cases.py; the script also reports the infinite-mean cases without replacing infinity by a finite cutoff.

Why the known-cutoff likelihood formula needs conditions¶

We prove the estimator stated above for n≥1n\ge1n≥1 iid exact Pareto observations, known xm>0x_m>0xm​>0, and observed xi≥xmx_i\ge x_mxi​≥xm​. Up to terms independent of α\alphaα, the log likelihood ℓ\ellℓ and its derivatives are

ℓ(α)=nlog⁡α−α∑i=1nlog⁡(xi/xm)+constant,ℓ′(α)=nα−∑i=1nlog⁡(xi/xm),ℓ′′(α)=−nα2<0.\begin{aligned} \ell(\alpha)&=n\log\alpha-\alpha\sum_{i=1}^n\log(x_i/x_m)+\text{constant},\\ \ell'(\alpha)&=\frac n\alpha-\sum_{i=1}^n\log(x_i/x_m),\\ \ell''(\alpha)&=-\frac n{\alpha^2}<0. \end{aligned}ℓ(α)ℓ′(α)ℓ′′(α)​=nlogα−αi=1∑n​log(xi​/xm​)+constant,=αn​−i=1∑n​log(xi​/xm​),=−α2n​<0.​
(16)

If ∑i=1nlog⁡(xi/xm)>0\sum_{i=1}^n\log(x_i/x_m)>0∑i=1n​log(xi​/xm​)>0, the unique maximizer is n/∑i=1nlog⁡(xi/xm)n/\sum_{i=1}^n\log(x_i/x_m)n/∑i=1n​log(xi​/xm​). If the sum is zero, every observation equals xmx_mxm​ and ℓ\ellℓ increases without bound as α→∞\alpha\to\inftyα→∞. Observations below xmx_mxm​ are outside this model’s support. A threshold estimated from the same sample changes the problem; this proof supplies no guarantee for that fit.

Sums and moment orders¶

Let X1,X2,…X_1,X_2,\ldotsX1​,X2​,… be iid Pareto Type I variables with the same α>0\alpha>0α>0 and xm>0x_m>0xm​>0, and put Sn=∑i=1nXiS_n=\sum_{i=1}^nX_iSn​=∑i=1n​Xi​ and Mn=max⁡1≤i≤nXiM_n=\max_{1\le i\le n}X_iMn​=max1≤i≤n​Xi​. For a growing sample, the max-to-sum ratio has three regimes:

  • If α>1\alpha>1α>1, then Mn/Sn→0M_n/S_n\to0Mn​/Sn​→0 almost surely. The linked finite-mean proof gives Sn/n→E[X]>0S_n/n\to\mathbb E[X]>0Sn​/n→E[X]>0 and Mn/n→0M_n/n\to0Mn​/n→0 almost surely, so their quotient tends to zero.

  • If 0<α<10<\alpha<10<α<1, then Mn/Sn→dRαM_n/S_n\xrightarrow{d}R_\alphaMn​/Sn​d​Rα​, where RαR_\alphaRα​ has a nondegenerate distribution on (0,1)(0,1)(0,1). In particular, the ratio does not tend to zero in probability, nor does it tend to one. This limit theorem is cited rather than proved here Darling, 1952, Theorem 5.1. Kevei and Mason (2014), p. 632 restate the iid result and give the corresponding sum/maximum limit law; our ratio is its reciprocal.

  • If α=1\alpha=1α=1, the mean is infinite but Mn/Sn→0M_n/S_n\to0Mn​/Sn​→0 in probability. More precisely, Mn/(xmn)M_n/(x_m n)Mn​/(xm​n) is bounded in probability and Sn/(xmnlog⁡n)→1S_n/(x_m n\log n)\to1Sn​/(xm​nlogn)→1 in probability. The calculation below proves these exact-Pareto assertions; it does not assert almost-sure convergence of the ratio.

For every α>0\alpha>0α>0, a different limit holds when the integer n≥1n\ge1n≥1 is fixed and the threshold grows:

P(Sn>x)∼P(Mn>x)∼nP(X>x),x→∞.\mathbb P(S_n>x)\sim\mathbb P(M_n>x) \sim n\mathbb P(X>x),\qquad x\to\infty.P(Sn​>x)∼P(Mn​>x)∼nP(X>x),x→∞.
(17)

This is the subexponential rare-event statement: a fixed-size sum exceeds a sufficiently high threshold mainly when one summand exceeds it. It holds even when α>1\alpha>1α>1 and the largest share vanishes along growing samples. For moments, the separate exact criterion is E[Xp]<∞\mathbb E[X^p]<\inftyE[Xp]<∞ if and only if p<αp<\alphap<α, for p>0p>0p>0, as proved in Pareto Moment Existence.

Exact-Pareto boundary calculation¶

We prove the two normalizations used above for α=1\alpha=1α=1. Without loss of generality, assume xm=1x_m=1xm​=1 within this calculation: divide each observation by the positive cutoff xmx_mxm​, and let XiX_iXi​, SnS_nSn​, and MnM_nMn​ now denote the rescaled observations, sum, and maximum. This scaling preserves Mn/SnM_n/S_nMn​/Sn​ and turns the two normalizations into Mn/nM_n/nMn​/n and Sn/(nlog⁡n)S_n/(n\log n)Sn​/(nlogn). For z>0z>0z>0 and sufficiently large nnn, independence gives

P ⁣(Mnn≤z)=(1−1nz)n⟶e−1/z.\mathbb P\!\left(\frac{M_n}{n}\le z\right) =\left(1-\frac{1}{nz}\right)^n\longrightarrow e^{-1/z}.P(nMn​​≤z)=(1−nz1​)n⟶e−1/z.
(18)

For the sum, truncate at nlog⁡nn\log nnlogn: for n≥3n\ge3n≥3, set Ti,n=Xi1{Xi≤nlog⁡n}T_{i,n}=X_i\mathbf1_{\{X_i\le n\log n\}}Ti,n​=Xi​1{Xi​≤nlogn}​. Integration of the density x−2x^{-2}x−2 on [1,nlog⁡n][1,n\log n][1,nlogn] gives E[Ti,n]=log⁡(nlog⁡n)\mathbb E[T_{i,n}]=\log(n\log n)E[Ti,n​]=log(nlogn) and E[Ti,n2]=nlog⁡n−1\mathbb E[T_{i,n}^2]=n\log n-1E[Ti,n2​]=nlogn−1. Hence

Var⁡ ⁣(∑i=1nTi,nnlog⁡n)≤nlog⁡nn(log⁡n)2=1log⁡n⟶0.\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\frac{\sum_{i=1}^nT_{i,n}}{n\log n}\right) \le\frac{n\log n}{n(\log n)^2}=\frac{1}{\log n}\longrightarrow0.Var(nlogn∑i=1n​Ti,n​​)≤n(logn)2nlogn​=logn1​⟶0.
(19)

The normalized expectation log⁡(nlog⁡n)/log⁡n\log(n\log n)/\log nlog(nlogn)/logn tends to 1. Chebyshev’s inequality gives convergence in probability for the truncated sum. The union bound P(Mn>nlog⁡n)≤n/(nlog⁡n)=1/log⁡n\mathbb P(M_n>n\log n)\le n/(n\log n)=1/\log nP(Mn​>nlogn)≤n/(nlogn)=1/logn transfers that convergence to Sn/(nlog⁡n)S_n/(n\log n)Sn​/(nlogn). Dividing the tight normalized maximum by this normalized sum and by log⁡n\log nlogn proves Mn/Sn→0M_n/S_n\to0Mn​/Sn​→0 in probability. Returning to the original units restores the normalizations Mn/(xmn)M_n/(x_m n)Mn​/(xm​n) and Sn/(xmnlog⁡n)S_n/(x_m n\log n)Sn​/(xm​nlogn); from here on, XiX_iXi​, SnS_nSn​, and MnM_nMn​ again denote the original, unscaled quantities.

Fixed-size rare-event calculation¶

We extend the two-summand bound on the subexponentiality page to prove the displayed fixed-nnn result. The case n=1n=1n=1 is immediate. For fixed n≥2n\ge2n≥2, choose h=xm(x/xm)γh=x_m(x/x_m)^\gammah=xm​(x/xm​)γ with 1/2<γ<11/2<\gamma<11/2<γ<1. If Sn>xS_n>xSn​>x but Mn≤xM_n\le xMn​≤x, either one observation lies in (x−(n−1)h,x](x-(n-1)h,x](x−(n−1)h,x], or at least two observations exceed hhh. Otherwise the sum is at most xxx. Thus

P(Sn>x, Mn≤x)≤n[Fˉ(x−(n−1)h)−Fˉ(x)]+(n2)Fˉ(h)2.\mathbb P(S_n>x,\ M_n\le x) \le n\bigl[\bar F(x-(n-1)h)-\bar F(x)\bigr] +\binom n2\bar F(h)^2.P(Sn​>x, Mn​≤x)≤n[Fˉ(x−(n−1)h)−Fˉ(x)]+(2n​)Fˉ(h)2.
(20)

After division by Fˉ(x)\bar F(x)Fˉ(x), the first bracket tends to zero because h/x→0h/x\to0h/x→0; the second tail ratio is (x/xm)α(1−2γ)→0(x/x_m)^{\alpha(1-2\gamma)}\to0(x/xm​)α(1−2γ)→0. Finally, P(Mn>x)=1−(1−Fˉ(x))n∼nFˉ(x)\mathbb P(M_n>x)=1-(1-\bar F(x))^n\sim n\bar F(x)P(Mn​>x)=1−(1−Fˉ(x))n∼nFˉ(x). Nonnegativity makes {Mn>x}\{M_n>x\}{Mn​>x} a subset of {Sn>x}\{S_n>x\}{Sn​>x}, and the negligible residual probability proves the sum-tail equivalence.

Positive sums and independent products¶

The sum and product discussions in SCoFT v4 §§5.2.1–5.2.2, pp. 98–100 Taleb, 2025, require different assumptions. Here we prove a bounded claim about sums and exact formulas for independent Pareto products.

Fix n<∞n<\inftyn<∞, positive weights wiw_iwi​, and nonnegative XiX_iXi​ with P(Xi>x)=x−αiLi(x)P(X_i>x)=x^{-\alpha_i}L_i(x)P(Xi​>x)=x−αi​Li​(x) eventually, where αi>0\alpha_i>0αi​>0 and each LiL_iLi​ is slowly varying. Dependence is unrestricted. For S=∑i=1nwiXiS=\sum_{i=1}^n w_iX_iS=∑i=1n​wi​Xi​,

max⁡iP(Xi>x/wi)≤P(S>x)≤∑i=1nP(Xi>x/(nwi)).\max_i P(X_i>x/w_i)\le P(S>x) \le\sum_{i=1}^nP(X_i>x/(nw_i)).imax​P(Xi​>x/wi​)≤P(S>x)≤i=1∑n​P(Xi​>x/(nwi​)).
(21)

The lower bound uses nonnegativity; the upper bound holds because a sum above xxx has some term above x/nx/nx/n. The logarithmic regular-variation consequence makes both bounds x−min⁡iαi+o(1)x^{-\min_i\alpha_i+o(1)}x−mini​αi​+o(1), so log⁡P(S>x)/log⁡x→−min⁡iαi\log P(S>x)/\log x\to-\min_i\alpha_ilogP(S>x)/logx→−mini​αi​. These bounds establish a logarithmic exponent, not a limiting survival constant or full regular variation of every dependent sum. If one allows signed variables, take a symmetric power-tailed VVV and (X1,X2)=(V,−V)(X_1,X_2)=(V,-V)(X1​,X2​)=(V,−V): both have right power tails but their sum is identically zero.

For products, let X1,X2X_1,X_2X1​,X2​ be independent unit-cutoff Pareto variables with exponents a,b>0a,b>0a,b>0. The symbols a,ba,ba,b are local exponents in this two-law calculation. For z≥1z\ge1z≥1, condition on X1X_1X1​ to obtain

P(X1X2>z)=z−a+az−b∫1ztb−a−1 dt={bz−a−az−bb−a,a≠b,z−a(1+alog⁡z),a=b.P(X_1X_2>z)=z^{-a}+a z^{-b}\int_1^z t^{b-a-1}\,dt =\begin{cases} \dfrac{b z^{-a}-a z^{-b}}{b-a},&a\ne b,\\[6pt] z^{-a}(1+a\log z),&a=b. \end{cases}P(X1​X2​>z)=z−a+az−b∫1z​tb−a−1dt=⎩⎨⎧​b−abz−a−az−b​,z−a(1+alogz),​a=b,a=b.​
(22)

For unequal exponents the smaller one determines the leading power. Equal exponents introduce a logarithmic factor, which is slowly varying but never constant. With a=1a=1a=1, b=2b=2b=2, the survival is 2/z−1/z22/z-1/z^22/z−1/z2; with a=b=1a=b=1a=b=1, it is (1+log⁡z)/z(1+\log z)/z(1+logz)/z. For other Pareto minima, apply the formula to X1X2/(xm,1xm,2)X_1X_2/(x_{m,1}x_{m,2})X1​X2​/(xm,1​xm,2​).

Independence cannot be suppressed: X2=X1X_2=X_1X2​=X1​ gives the square, with exponent a/2a/2a/2. Multiplication by a dependent bounded variable can even remove the tail: X2=1/X1X_2=1/X_1X2​=1/X1​ gives product one. Claims that multiplication always preserves the heavier tail therefore need additional hypotheses. The power-transformation proof handles deterministic powers separately.

Use pareto_product_logsf.

import numpy as np
from xmath.incerto.power_laws import pareto_product_logsf

for a, b in ((1, 2), (1, 1)):
    survival = np.exp(pareto_product_logsf(np.log([1, 10, 100]), a, b))
    print(f"a={a:d}, b={b:d}: [" + ", ".join(f"{v:.4g}" for v in survival) + "]")

Output

a=1, b=2: [1, 0.19, 0.0199]
a=1, b=1: [1, 0.3303, 0.05605]

Equal exponents introduce the logarithmic factor derived above.

Figure regeneration: uv run python demos/incerto/power_laws.py for these product survivals, the moment-integral figure, and exact population checks. This adds no new growing-sample dominance claim; the earlier three max-to-sum regimes remain unchanged.

Caveats¶

  • Empirical data rarely follows an exact Pareto law from its minimum value. A tail model needs a threshold choice, diagnostic plots, and sensitivity checks.

  • A finite theoretical mean can still be practically hard to estimate when α\alphaα is close to 1. The issue is pre-asymptotic behavior, not merely the formal existence of E[X]\mathbb E[X]E[X].

  • The exact failure mode depends on the moment order. As the upper cutoff b≥xmb\ge x_mb≥xm​ tends to infinity, the cutoff moment grows like log⁡b\log blogb at p=αp=\alphap=α and like bp−αb^{p-\alpha}bp−α for p>αp>\alphap>α.

  • Do not estimate high moments of heavy-tailed samples without checking whether those moments are implied by the fitted tail exponent.

A rare Pareto regime retains its power tail¶

The regime question in SCoFT v4 appendix A, §A.1, pp. 122–124 Taleb, 2025, does not by itself specify a Pareto law. Here is an example that does. With probability w∈(0,1]w\in(0,1]w∈(0,1], draw a Pareto variable with cutoff xm>0x_m>0xm​>0 and exponent α>0\alpha>0α>0; otherwise draw a uniform variable on [0,xm][0,x_m][0,xm​]. For u≥xmu\ge x_mu≥xm​, conditioning on the regime proves

P(X>u)=w(xm/u)α.P(X>u)=w(x_m/u)^\alpha.P(X>u)=w(xm​/u)α.
(23)

For every positive order qqq, the mixture moment is (1−w)xmq/(q+1)+wE[XParetoq](1-w)x_m^q/(q+1)+w\mathbb E[X_{\rm Pareto}^q](1−w)xmq​/(q+1)+wE[XParetoq​]. The existing moment proof therefore implies finiteness exactly when q<αq<\alphaq<α. A small positive mixture weight changes the survival constant but not the exponent or moment gate. At w=0w=0w=0 the model becomes bounded and all positive moments exist.

With w=0.02w=0.02w=0.02, xm=1x_m=1xm​=1, α=3/2\alpha=3/2α=3/2, survival at u=4u=4u=4 is 0.0025, the mean is 0.55, and the second moment is infinite. These are population values; they do not predict which tail observations will occur in a small sample. The catalog’s normal location mixture has a different tail class even when its regimes are widely separated. The chapter-6 demo prints this example without sampling or clipping it.
